cweDef.name: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File
cweDef.summary: Passwords, tokens, or secrets are written to logs, where retention and access controls rarely match their sensitivity.

title: Sensitive value in log call ({lang}) — review required
description: A {lang} log call outputs a value named like a credential: {sink}. Logs persist, replicate, and are read by operators and tools that must never see secrets. This lexical rule flags the call; the reviewer confirms the value is non-sensitive or redacts it.
remediation: Stop logging the value; log {safe} instead, and scrub historic logs that already hold it.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches credential-adjacent names in log calls regardless of actual content.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on credential-named values in {lang} log calls.
fp: Logging field names, lengths, or presence flags (not values) is the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} places a credential-named value on a log line. Log pipelines retain data for months and expose it to support tooling, so logged secrets effectively become shared. The remedy is logging {safe}.
applicability: {lang} codebases emitting logs; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Credential disclosure to log readers and retention stores; MEDIUM severity, HIGH when logs ship to third parties.
why: {lang} log calls output credential-named values ({sink}), which persist in log stores.
fix: Remove the value from the log call; emit {safe}.
Rotate any credential already written to logs.
Re-run the scan and confirm no credential-named value remains in log calls.
verifyT: Rescan shows no credential-named value in log calls, and log samples hold no secrets.

title: Client-side or header redirect to computed address ({lang}) — review required
description: A {lang} redirect assigns a computed address: {sink}. Untrusted input in the address turns the site into a phishing springboard. This lexical rule flags the assignment; the reviewer confirms the target is fixed or validated.
remediation: Allow only relative paths or listed hosts ({safe}) before redirecting.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: any computed redirect target matches. Call-shaped redirects are separate rules.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on computed redirect targets in {lang} code.
fp: Appending trusted tracking parameters to a fixed URL is the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} navigates to a computed address. Client-side and header redirects are as abusable as server-side ones when input shapes the target. The remedy is target validation via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} code assigning redirect targets; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Phishing via trusted-domain links; MEDIUM severity.
why: {lang} redirects navigate to computed addresses ({sink}), so untrusted input enables phishing.
fix: Validate the target with {safe}.
Drop untrusted redirect parameters in favor of fixed destinations.
Re-run the scan and confirm no open target remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no open redirect, and hostile targets are rejected.

cweDef.name: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
cweDef.summary: The server fetches a URL built from input, so attackers reach internal services and cloud metadata.

title: Server-side fetch of assembled URL ({lang}) — review required
description: A {lang} HTTP client fetches a URL assembled from parts: {sink}. Untrusted input in the URL reaches internal hosts, metadata endpoints, and file URLs. This lexical rule flags the fetch; the reviewer confirms the host is fixed or allowlisted.
remediation: Fetch only allowlisted hosts ({safe}); block metadata ranges, localhost, and non-HTTP schemes, and disable redirects or re-validate them.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: any assembled fetch URL matches, including trusted ones.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on assembled fetch URLs in {lang} code.
fp: Assembling fixed API paths on a fixed host is the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} makes the server issue a request to a computed URL. SSRF weaponizes the server's network position: cloud metadata, internal admin ports, and intranet hosts. The remedy is host allowlisting via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} server code fetching URLs; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Internal network access and credential theft via metadata endpoints; HIGH severity.
why: {lang} server fetches assemble URLs from parts ({sink}), so untrusted input reaches internal hosts.
fix: Restrict fetch hosts with {safe}, blocking metadata, localhost, and private ranges.
Block file/gopher/dict schemes and re-validate redirect targets.
Re-run the scan and confirm no open fetch remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no open fetch, and metadata/internal probes are refused.

title: JWT 'none' algorithm ({lang}) — review required
description: Configuration or code in {lang} names the JWT 'none' algorithm: {sink}. Tokens without signatures are accepted as genuine, so anyone can mint them. This lexical rule flags the name; the reviewer confirms it is test-only or removes it.
remediation: Require a signature algorithm ({safe}) and reject 'none' explicitly in verification.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the name regardless of context.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on the JWT 'none' name in {lang} code or config.
fp: Test vectors demonstrating rejection of 'none' are the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} names unsecured JWTs. The 'none' algorithm exists for special cases, but verifiers that accept it let attackers forge any claim. The remedy is pinning {safe}.
applicability: {lang} JWT verification configuration; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Authentication bypass via self-minted tokens; HIGH severity.
why: {lang} JWT handling names the 'none' algorithm ({sink}), so unsigned tokens verify as genuine.
fix: Pin verification to {safe} and reject 'none' explicitly.
Audit issuers to confirm none mint unsigned tokens.
Re-run the scan and confirm no 'none' remains outside rejection tests.
verifyT: Rescan shows no 'none' outside rejection tests, and unsigned tokens are refused.

title: XML parser with entities enabled ({lang}) — review required
description: An XML parser in {lang} is configured to resolve entities or load DTDs: {sink}. External entities in untrusted XML then read files and probe networks. This lexical rule flags the setting; the reviewer confirms the input is trusted or disables entities.
remediation: Disable DTDs and external entities ({safe}) for any XML crossing a trust boundary.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the setting regardless of input trust. Factory-call XXE sinks are separate rules.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on entity-enabling XML settings in {lang} code.
fp: Parsing trusted local configuration is the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} switches entity processing on. XXE payloads abuse doctypes to exfiltrate files and scan networks through the parser's authority. The remedy is disabling entities via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} XML parsing configuration; single-line lexical scope.
risk: File disclosure and SSRF through malicious XML; HIGH severity.
why: {lang} XML parsing enables entities ({sink}), so hostile documents read files and probe networks.
fix: Apply {safe} to every XML parser on untrusted input.
Prefer data formats without entity features for new interfaces.
Re-run the scan and confirm no entity-enabling setting remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no entity-enabling setting, and XXE probes resolve to nothing.

cweDef.name: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
cweDef.summary: State-changing requests lack unguessable tokens, so attacker sites ride the victim's session.

title: CSRF protection disabled ({lang}) — review required
description: CSRF protection is switched off in {lang}: {sink}. State-changing endpoints then accept requests forged by attacker sites riding the victim's session. This lexical rule flags the switch; the reviewer confirms the endpoint is safe or re-enables protection.
remediation: Re-enable CSRF checks ({safe}); exempt only safe, unauthenticated, or token-authenticated endpoints with a recorded reason.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the switch regardless of endpoint sensitivity.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on CSRF-disabling settings in {lang} code.
fp: Stateless token-authenticated APIs are the common false positive — confirm no cookie session exists.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} removes the unguessable-token check browsers cannot forge. Exempted endpoints trust ambient credentials alone. The remedy is restoring {safe}.
applicability: {lang} web handlers and configuration; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Cross-site request forgery on state-changing endpoints; MEDIUM severity, HIGH for account and payment actions.
why: {lang} CSRF protection is disabled ({sink}), so attacker sites can forge state-changing requests.
fix: Restore {safe} on the endpoint.
If the endpoint must stay exempt, record why ambient credentials cannot abuse it.
Re-run the scan and confirm no unjustified exemption remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no unjustified exemption, and forged cross-site requests are rejected.

title: Credential compared to a literal ({lang}) — review required
description: A credential-named value is compared to a quoted literal: {sink}. Hardcoded comparison secrets ship in source and binaries, and rotation needs a release. This lexical rule flags the comparison; the reviewer confirms it is test-only or moves the secret out.
remediation: Compare against a value from {safe} and rotate the exposed literal.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches literal comparisons regardless of environment. Generic secret assignments are separate rules.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on credential-to-literal comparisons in {lang} code.
fp: Test fixtures comparing against dummy values are the common false positive.
recordDesc: Comparing a credential to a source literal ({sink}) bakes the secret into every checkout and build. The remedy is loading the expected value from {safe}.
risk: Exposed secrets and unrotatable credentials; MEDIUM severity, HIGH when the literal guards production.
why: {lang} credentials compare against source literals ({sink}), which leak through checkouts and builds.
fix: Load the expected value from {safe} and compare in constant time.
Rotate the literal that was committed.
Re-run the scan and confirm no literal comparison remains outside tests.
verifyT: Rescan shows no literal comparison outside tests, and rotation is complete.

java: a secret manager or KDF-verified hash

cweDef.name: Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information
cweDef.summary: Stack traces and debug errors leak paths, versions, and internals to whoever can trigger them.

title: Stack trace or debug error printed ({lang}) — review required
description: Code in {lang} prints a stack trace or debug error: {sink}. Traces leak paths, versions, library names, and code structure to whoever can trigger them. This lexical rule flags the print; the reviewer confirms it never reaches untrusted output.
remediation: Log a correlation id with {safe} and show users a generic message; keep traces server-side.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the print regardless of output destination.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on trace-printing calls in {lang} code.
fp: CLI tools printing traces to their own operator are the common false positive.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} serializes internals into an error channel. Attackers harvest traces for reconnaissance before deeper attacks. The remedy is generic user errors plus {safe}.
risk: Reconnaissance disclosure; LOW severity, higher on public endpoints.
why: {lang} error paths print traces ({sink}), disclosing internals to whoever triggers them.
fix: Replace the print with {safe} plus a generic user message.
Keep full traces in server logs only.
Re-run the scan and confirm no trace print reaches responses.
verifyT: Rescan shows no trace print on response paths, and error probes return generic text.

cweDef.name: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes
cweDef.summary: Request fields bind directly to object attributes, so clients set privileged properties.

title: Request data bound wholesale ({lang}) — review required
description: Request data is copied onto an object without a field list: {sink}. Clients can then set privileged attributes (roles, flags, ownership) the form never showed. This lexical rule flags the binding; the reviewer confirms an allowlist or picks fields explicitly.
remediation: Bind through {safe}, assigning only listed fields from the request.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches wholesale binding regardless of model guards.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on wholesale request binding in {lang} code.
fp: Models with framework-level guarded attributes are the common false positive — confirm the guard.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} merges every request field into an object. Mass assignment turns hidden model attributes into client-writable inputs. The remedy is explicit binding via {safe}.
applicability: {lang} request handlers binding input to models; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Privilege escalation via hidden fields (is_admin, role); MEDIUM severity, HIGH on account objects.
why: {lang} request data binds wholesale ({sink}), so clients can set privileged attributes.
fix: Replace wholesale binding with {safe}.
Add framework guarded/fillable lists as defense in depth.
Re-run the scan and confirm no wholesale binding remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no wholesale binding, and privileged-field probes are ignored.

cweDef.name: Generation of Predictable IV with CBC Mode
cweDef.summary: A fixed initialization vector makes equal plaintexts encrypt equally, leaking patterns.

title: Hardcoded IV or nonce ({lang}) — review required
description: An initialization vector or nonce is assigned a fixed literal: {sink}. Reused IVs make equal plaintexts encrypt equally and can destroy the security of stream-like modes. This lexical rule flags the literal; the reviewer confirms uniqueness or generates it randomly.
remediation: Generate a fresh random IV per message ({safe}) and store it alongside the ciphertext.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches literal IVs regardless of cipher mode.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on literal IV or nonce assignments.
fp: Test vectors with fixed IVs are the common false positive — confirm test-only scope.
recordDesc: A fixed IV ({sink}) repeats across messages, so patterns survive encryption and GCM-style modes fail catastrophically. Fresh randomness per message ({safe}) is the remedy.
applicability: Encryption setup code assigning IVs or nonces; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Pattern leakage and, for nonce-misuse-sensitive modes, full break; MEDIUM severity, HIGH for GCM/CTR reuse.
why: Encryption uses a hardcoded IV ({sink}), so ciphertext patterns leak and nonce-reuse breaks modes.
fix: Generate the IV randomly per message with {safe}.
Store the IV with the ciphertext; never reuse a (key, IV) pair.
Re-run the scan and confirm no literal IV remains outside test vectors.
verifyT: Rescan shows no literal IV outside test vectors, and captures show unique IVs.

cweDef.name: Use of Externally-Controlled Format String
cweDef.summary: A variable format string lets attackers read and write memory through conversion specifiers.

title: Variable format string ({lang}) — review required
description: A {lang} formatting call uses a variable as its format string: {sink}. Conversion specifiers in the value read and write process memory. This lexical rule flags the call; the reviewer confirms the value is fixed or passes it as an argument.
remediation: Use a fixed format string ({safe}) and pass the value as an argument.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches a variable-only call to the named formatter; fixed formats with variable arguments never match, and identifiers that merely end in the formatter name (for example sprintf wrappers around printf) are outside this rule.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on variable format strings in {lang} code.
fp: Wrapper functions forwarding a trusted format are the common false positive — confirm the source.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} interprets a variable as format text. Specifiers like %x and %n turn output routines into memory disclosure and write primitives. The remedy is fixed formats ({safe}).
risk: Memory disclosure and write; HIGH severity where the value is remotely influenced.
why: {lang} formatting interprets a variable as format text ({sink}), enabling specifier attacks.
fix: Replace the variable format with {safe}, passing the value as an argument.
Enable compiler format warnings to catch regressions.
Re-run the scan and confirm no variable format remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no variable format, and specifier probes print literally.

title: Credential noted in a work comment ({lang}) — review required
description: A work-item comment names a credential with a value: {sink}. Comments ship to every checkout and are rarely scrubbed, so noted secrets persist indefinitely. This lexical rule flags the note; the reviewer confirms no live value or rotates it.
remediation: Remove the value from the comment; track the work in {safe} without secrets.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches credential-adjacent notes regardless of value liveness.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on credential notes in comments.
fp: Placeholder-shaped notes (changeme, xxx) are the common false positive.
recordDesc: A comment noting a credential ({sink}) distributes the value to every reader and archive of the source. Comments lack the handling controls of secret stores. The remedy is value-free tracking via {safe}.
risk: Secret persistence in history and checkouts; LOW severity, raised when the value is live.
why: Work comments note credential values ({sink}), which persist in every checkout.
fix: Delete the value from the comment; keep only the task.
Rotate the value if it was ever live.
Re-run the scan and confirm no credential note remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no credential note, and history scrubbing is complete where needed.

universal: a secret manager plus a value-free ticket

title: Cleartext http:// URL ({lang}) — review required
description: Code references a cleartext HTTP URL: {sink}. Traffic to it is readable and modifiable by network observers. This lexical rule flags the literal; the reviewer confirms the endpoint is non-sensitive or upgrades it.
remediation: Use the https:// equivalent ({safe}); keep http only for non-sensitive local endpoints with a comment.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the scheme regardless of endpoint sensitivity.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on http:// literals.
fp: Localhost, documentation links, and legacy device endpoints are the common false positives.
recordDesc: A cleartext URL ({sink}) sends bytes without confidentiality or integrity. Passive observers read credentials and tokens; active ones rewrite responses. The remedy is the https equivalent ({safe}).
risk: Eavesdropping and tampering; LOW severity, raised for authenticated or sensitive endpoints.
why: Code references cleartext HTTP ({sink}), exposing the traffic to observers.
fix: Replace the URL with {safe}.
For endpoints without TLS, document the exception and its compensating controls.
Re-run the scan and confirm no sensitive cleartext URL remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no sensitive cleartext URL, and traffic captures show TLS.

title: Cleartext ws:// URL ({lang}) — review required
description: Code references a cleartext WebSocket URL: {sink}. Frames to it are readable and modifiable by network observers. This lexical rule flags the literal; the reviewer confirms the channel is non-sensitive or upgrades it.
remediation: Use the wss:// equivalent ({safe}).
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the scheme regardless of channel sensitivity.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on ws:// literals.
fp: Local development sockets are the common false positive.
recordDesc: A cleartext WebSocket URL ({sink}) carries frames without TLS. Session cookies and messages on the socket are exposed. The remedy is wss ({safe}).
risk: Eavesdropping and tampering on the socket; LOW severity, raised for authenticated channels.
why: Code references cleartext WebSockets ({sink}), exposing frames to observers.
fix: Replace the URL with {safe}.
For local-only sockets, document the exception.
Re-run the scan and confirm no sensitive cleartext socket remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no sensitive cleartext socket, and captures show TLS.

title: Download piped to shell ({lang}) — review required
description: A download is piped straight into a shell: {sink}. The executed bytes are whatever the network returned — tampering, truncation, or a compromised server runs attacker code. This lexical rule flags the pipe; the reviewer confirms verification or removes it.
remediation: Download, verify ({safe}), then execute as separate steps; never pipe network bytes to a shell.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the pipe regardless of transport or verification.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on download-to-shell pipes in {lang} scripts.
fp: Pipes over verified local files (not network) are the common false positive — confirm the source.
recordDesc: Piping a download into a shell ({sink}) executes unverified network bytes with the user's authority. TLS alone does not make this safe: server compromise or partial reads still execute. The remedy is fetch-verify-run ({safe}).
applicability: {lang} install scripts and runbooks; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Remote code execution on installer runs; HIGH severity.
why: Downloads pipe into a shell ({sink}), executing unverified network bytes.
fix: Split into download, verify with {safe}, then run.
Pin releases by version and checksum.
Re-run the scan and confirm no download-to-shell pipe remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no download-to-shell pipe, and installs verify before running.

title: Passwordless sudo grant ({lang}) — review required
description: Sudoers configuration grants passwordless execution: {sink}. Any process as that user gains the listed privileges without authentication, so one compromised account or script escalates silently. This lexical rule flags the grant; the reviewer confirms the scope is minimal or requires a password.
remediation: Scope the grant to exact binaries ({safe}) or drop NOPASSWD so authentication gates it.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the tag regardless of command scope.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on NOPASSWD grants in sudoers configuration.
fp: Automation accounts restricted to exact [(]non-shell[)] binaries are the common (accepted) case — confirm the list.
recordDesc: A NOPASSWD sudo grant ({sink}) removes the authentication step from privilege escalation. Combined with broad commands it hands root to any process running as the user. The remedy is exact-command scoping ({safe}).
risk: Silent privilege escalation; HIGH severity, critical with ALL commands.
why: Sudo grants passwordless execution ({sink}), so compromise of the account silently escalates.
fix: Restrict the grant with {safe} to exact binaries, never ALL.
Prefer requiring a password where automation allows.
Re-run the scan and confirm no broad NOPASSWD remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no broad NOPASSWD, and sudo -l audits minimal.

title: Setuid bit set ({lang}) — review required
description: A file gains the setuid bit: {sink}. It then runs with the owner's privileges for every caller, so any flaw in it becomes privilege escalation. This lexical rule flags the bit; the reviewer confirms the binary is minimal and audited or drops the bit.
remediation: Drop setuid in favor of {safe}; if it must stay, minimize the binary and audit it.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the bit regardless of binary safety.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on setuid grants in {lang} scripts.
fp: System utilities designed for setuid are the common accepted case.
recordDesc: Setting setuid ({sink}) promotes every caller to the file owner's privileges while the binary runs. Memory flaws, path handling, and environment inheritance all become escalation vectors. The remedy is capability-based design ({safe}).
risk: Local privilege escalation through the binary; MEDIUM severity, HIGH for custom setuid code.
why: Files gain setuid ({sink}), running every caller with the owner's privileges.
fix: Replace setuid with {safe}.
If setuid must stay, shrink the binary and audit its inputs.
Re-run the scan and confirm no unjustified setuid remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no unjustified setuid, and find audits no unexpected setuid files.

shell: capabilities or a privileged helper service

cweDef.name: Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort
cweDef.summary: Fast password hashing lets attackers test billions of guesses per second on stolen hashes.

title: PBKDF2 with low iteration count ({lang}) — review required
description: PBKDF2 is configured with a small iteration count: {sink}. Low effort lets attackers brute-force stolen hashes cheaply. This lexical rule flags counts under five digits; the reviewer confirms the value meets current guidance or raises it.
remediation: Raise the count to {safe} or switch to a memory-hard function.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches small numeric counts; variable-driven counts are missed.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on PBKDF2 iteration counts in {lang} code.
fp: Test-only hashes are the common false positive — confirm test scope.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} sets PBKDF2's work factor. Iteration counts that were fine a decade ago now fall to GPUs in hours. Current guidance ({safe}) restores the cost asymmetry. The remedy is raising the count.
risk: Cheap offline cracking of stolen hashes; MEDIUM severity.
why: {lang} PBKDF2 uses a low iteration count ({sink}), making stolen hashes cheap to crack.
fix: Raise iterations to {safe}.
Consider argon2/scrypt for new systems.
Re-run the scan and confirm no low count remains outside tests.
verifyT: Rescan shows no low count outside tests, and hashing cost benchmarks meet policy.

title: bcrypt with low cost ({lang}) — review required
description: bcrypt is configured with a single-digit cost: {sink}. Low cost makes stolen hashes cheap to crack. This lexical rule flags the value; the reviewer confirms it meets policy or raises it.
remediation: Raise the cost to {safe}.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches small numeric costs; variable-driven costs are missed.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on bcrypt cost in {lang} code.
fp: Test-only hashes are the common false positive — confirm test scope.
recordDesc: In {lang}, {sink} sets bcrypt's cost factor. Each increment doubles attacker work; single-digit costs fall quickly. The remedy is raising to {safe}.
risk: Cheap offline cracking; LOW severity (single-digit costs are usually tests).
why: {lang} bcrypt uses a low cost ({sink}), making stolen hashes cheap to crack.
fix: Raise the cost to {safe}.
Re-hash existing passwords at next login.
Re-run the scan and confirm no low cost remains outside tests.
verifyT: Rescan shows no low cost outside tests.

cweDef.name: Weak Password Requirements
cweDef.summary: Short minimum lengths let users pick passwords that fall to guessing and cracking.

title: Short password minimum length ({lang}) — review required
description: A password length floor is set below eight characters: {sink}. Short minimums let users pick guessable passwords. This lexical rule flags the value; the reviewer confirms policy or raises it.
remediation: Raise the minimum to {safe} and check chosen passwords against breach lists.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches small numeric floors; variable-driven floors are missed.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on password length floors in {lang} code or markup.
fp: Non-password fields sharing the attribute are the common false positive — confirm the field.
recordDesc: A length floor under eight ({sink}) permits the weakest common passwords. Length is the cheapest password defense; the remedy is raising to {safe}.
applicability: {lang} signup and credential forms; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Guessable user passwords; LOW severity (one control among several).
why: Password minimums below eight characters ({sink}) permit guessable passwords.
fix: Raise the floor to {safe}.
Add breach-list screening for chosen passwords.
Re-run the scan and confirm no short floor remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no short floor, and short passwords are rejected.

cweDef.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
cweDef.summary: Sensitive data reaches parties who should never see it, through logs, errors, or metadata.

title: Unsafe referrer policy ({lang}) — review required
description: A page sets the most permissive referrer policy: {sink}. Full URLs — including tokens and ids in query strings — leak to every linked site. This lexical rule flags the policy; the reviewer confirms no sensitive query data or tightens it.
remediation: Set {safe} so cross-origin links carry no full URL.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the policy regardless of URL sensitivity.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on referrer policy in {lang} markup.
fp: Pages with no sensitive query data are the common accepted case.
recordDesc: An unsafe-url referrer policy ({sink}) attaches the full page URL to outbound requests. Query strings routinely hold session-adjacent data. The remedy is {safe}.
risk: URL disclosure to third parties; LOW severity.
why: Pages send full URLs as referrers ({sink}), leaking query data to linked sites.
fix: Set the policy to {safe}.
Move sensitive values out of query strings regardless.
Re-run the scan and confirm no unsafe policy remains.
verifyT: Rescan shows no unsafe policy, and outbound requests carry trimmed referrers.

title: Obsolete TLS/SSL version named ({lang}) — review required
description: Configuration or code names an obsolete protocol version: {sink}. SSLv2/SSLv3 and TLS 1.0/1.1 are broken or deprecated; negotiating them exposes connections to known attacks. This lexical rule flags the name; the reviewer confirms it is documentation or removes it.
remediation: Require {safe} and drop the obsolete name.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the name regardless of context (code, config, or prose).
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on obsolete protocol names.
fp: Changelog and documentation mentions are the common false positive.
recordDesc: Naming {sink} keeps a broken protocol negotiable or documents its acceptance. Each obsolete version carries practical attacks (POODLE, BEAST-class, weak record handling). The remedy is {safe}.
applicability: TLS configuration and version checks; single-line lexical scope.
risk: Downgrade to broken protocols; MEDIUM severity.
why: Obsolete protocol versions ({sink}) stay negotiable, exposing connections to known attacks.
fix: Require {safe} and remove the obsolete name.
Test that handshakes reject the old versions.
Re-run the scan and confirm no obsolete name remains outside prose.
verifyT: Rescan shows no obsolete name outside prose, and old-version handshakes fail.

title: Weak cipher named ({lang}) — review required
description: Configuration or code names a weak cipher: {sink}. RC4, single DES, and 3DES are broken or deprecated for protecting data. This lexical rule flags the name; the reviewer confirms it is documentation or removes it.
remediation: Negotiate {safe} and drop the weak name.
limitation: Lexical, line-based: matches the name regardless of context.
scopeT: Single-line lexical match on weak cipher names.
fp: Documentation and compatibility lists are the common false positive.
recordDesc: Naming {sink} keeps a weak cipher available for negotiation or use. RC4 biases, DES key size, and 3DES block size each ended these ciphers' suitability. The remedy is {safe}.
risk: Confidentiality loss under a weak cipher; MEDIUM severity.
why: Weak ciphers ({sink}) stay available, so connections may negotiate broken encryption.
fix: Restrict negotiation to {safe}.
Verify weak ciphers are refused in handshakes.
Re-run the scan and confirm no weak name remains outside prose.
verifyT: Rescan shows no weak name outside prose, and weak-cipher handshakes fail.
